A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Perception-as-Control and provide readable text, equations, figures, and references. V1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Appendices A–E. The complete supplied material supports comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original generated-video demonstrations for camera, object, and collaborative motion control and application examples in Sections 4.2–4.3 and Figures 4–7.

after.justification: V2 reports original quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–4, alongside generated examples and failure cases in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The central representation, U-Net/ReferenceNet framework, loss, and three-stage training procedure are retained. V2 adds MotionCtrl++ and CameraCtrl++ adaptations, integrating rendered camera/object signals through separate encoders and fusion into SVD-based implementations (Section 4.2, Appendix B, Figure 13). These extend the method without replacing its core.

E1.justification: RealEstate10K, WebVid10M, and the existing animation applications remain. V2 extends qualitative test scenarios with explicit large-orbit camera stress cases and object-rotation/human-walking failure cases (Figures 5 and 16). The larger reported training sample counts change settings rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V1 discusses competitors but presents no evaluated head-to-head comparisons. V2 evaluates CameraCtrl, reproduced CameraCtrl*, MotionCtrl, and their ++ adaptations for camera control (Table 1), and Motion-I2V, MOFA-Video, and the ++ adaptations for object control (Table 2). Figures 5–6 add qualitative baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 introduces quantitative evaluation on 1K test clips from each dataset, six quality/controllability metrics, frame-count comparison variants, and controlled ablation protocols. Section 4.1 also revises reported training sizes from approximately 6K/35K to 61K/352K RealEstate/WebVid clips. The PDFs do not establish whether these size revisions reflect expanded training or corrected reporting.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation ablations comparing point offsets, point positions, 3D spheres, and spheres plus the world envelope, and compares one-, two-, and three-stage training (Tables 3–4, Figure 7, Appendix C). It also adds a controlled focal-length comparison and concrete rotation/human-motion failure analyses (Figures 10 and 16), beyond v1's demonstrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. V2's new quantitative tables provide point estimates without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds the first quantitative results: Table 2 reports Ours FVD 161.076 and ObjMC 23.32, while Table 4 reports FVD 318.941, 254.907, and 161.076 for one-, two-, and three-stage training. Comparative examples and failure findings are also added. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, noise-prediction objective, and mathematical substance of the sphere/camera construction remain unchanged. V2 clarifies frame versus diffusion-timestep symbols and other notation; it adds no substantive derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The central claims about fine-grained collaborative control and four motion-related applications remain. V2 adds an explicit contribution claim that the representation is independent of base-model architecture and consistently improves controllability across benchmarks. Its conclusion also narrows the contrast with prior work to coarse or inflexible collaborative control.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations linking spatial alignment, depth, the world envelope, and staged training to the ablation outcomes (Section 4.3). Appendix E newly identifies limitations in representing rotation, producing realistic human locomotion, and dependence on preprocessing estimators, supported by failure examples. V1 contains no comparable limitations analysis.

D1.justification: V2 newly names PySceneDetect and discloses learning rates of 1e-5 for stages 1–2 and 1e-6 for stage 3. It revises reported hardware from eight A100 GPUs to one and adds integration, training, and application diagrams in Appendices B–D. These improve documentation; the newly disclosed learning rates do not establish a training-setting change.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for FID, FVD, VBench, and PySceneDetect while retaining the main related-work coverage. Research positioning is refined by acknowledging prior collaborative controllers and distinguishing the proposed approach through control granularity, flexibility, and compatibility with other frameworks.

P1.justification: V2 extensively tightens the introduction and method explanations and reorganizes the experimental narrative around comparisons and ablations. Much of v1's case-study and application discussion is relocated and expanded in Appendices A and D, producing a substantially different document structure.

P2.justification: V2 substantially rebuilds the visual presentation with Tables 1–4, comparative and ablation figures, architecture/training/application diagrams, and failure panels. Earlier qualitative examples are selectively combined in the main text and expanded or rearranged in Figures 9–12; these are not all newly introduced results.

improvement.justification: V1's claims relied on selected demonstrations without evaluated competitors or ablations. V2 substantially resolves that evidentiary weakness through defined test-set evaluations, baseline comparisons, component/training ablations, and concrete limitations. Reporting remains imperfect: CameraCtrl*++ has worse translation error than CameraCtrl* (0.291 versus 0.257), qualifying the broad improvement language, and Ours SubCon differs between Table 2 (0.968) and Tables 3–4 (0.969). These limited issues do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and applicability assessment.
